notes.3: This question involved calculating average speed, and many weaker candidates used the average value of the maximum and minimum speed to obtain option C rather than dividing the total distance by the total time.
notes.4: Although a large proportion of candidates of all abilities coped well with this question, a common error for the less able was to confuse weight with density, thus arriving at option C .
notes.6: In this generally well-answered question the most popular distractor was D ; this showed a situation with zero resultant force, but not zero turning effect.
notes.7: The common mistake in this question was to choose the extra extension produced by increasing the load from 2.0 N to 3.0 N (option B ), rather than the total extension.
notes.13: Option B was a popular distractor, despite the fact that this showed zero starting pressure.
notes.17: Some candidates believed that warm air would flow away from the heater under the cupboard.
notes.21: This question on the electromagnetic spectrum showed that most candidates were either unaware that infra- red causes the most heating, or that it is positioned just beyond the red end of the visible spectrum; many chose position B .
notes.25: This example of the effect of magnetic attraction was new to most candidates, and most responses were incorrect.
notes.26: A significant number of the weaker candidates chose option C in this question. As this is the exact opposite of the correct response, it is possible that these candidates were unclear about the meaning of ‘open’ and ‘closed’ with reference to a switch, even though the question was carefully worded to help any who were unsure about this.
notes.32: Able candidates had little difficulty with this question about a potential divider, but others were unable to use the 1:2 ratio of the resistor values to arrive at a value of 8.0 V across the 20 Ω resistor. Most either thought that the voltage would be split evenly between the two resistors, or that each would receive the full 12 V.
notes.35: Many of the weaker candidates believed that high-voltage transmission made the process faster.
